rv.q: That we believe this, and remain in his thrall, is Mr. Langella’s personal triumph.

Rattigan wrote stronger plays than 'Man and Boy,' 'The Deep Blue Sea' and 'Separate Tables' in particular, and he would have been even better served had the Roundabout revived one of them instead. Nor does this production, save for Mr. Langella's ennobling presence and Ms. Aitken's shrewd cuts, make the best possible case for 'Man and Boy.
Dare you to take your eyes off him.

What emerges is a somewhat clunky and sometimes limp seven-character play about the complicated relationship between fathers and sons that gets a surge of electricity whenever Langella — at his fussy, oily best — appears.
Too bad: "Man and Boy" isn't a great play, but with equal sparring partners, it could have been a very good show.
But they don't disguise the fact that this is a second-rate play.

The thematic undercurrents of socialism versus capitalism as applied in a time of crisis, the pervasive agony that's trying to bust down the doors of Basil's apartment, and the charismatic greasiness of Gregor speak for themselves and our time with no extra assistance required.
Indeed, in every detail, he’s The Man.
Mostly, the production is an opportunity to see strong dramatic performances.

Luckily, this production, which opened Sunday at Broadway's Theatre, has a miracle worker in Frank Langella, whose predictably sumptuous performance mitigates not only Gregor's ickiness but the play's shortcomings.

In spite of the confused second act, this 'Man and Boy' has a strong balance sheet, thanks mostly to Langella. As he did in 'Frost/Nixon,' Langella creates an irresistibly strong leader who draws us to him despite his despicable actions.
Regrettably, the neatness, like the play's dramatic interest, begins and ends there.
But even a triple Tony-winning powerhouse can’t make damp gunpowder flash and ignite.
The fall theater season has barely started, and, already, a strong candidate for worst show of the year has emerged.
Langella delivers a performance of masterful comic timing and physicality that is endlessly entertaining.

Maria Aitken has decently directed a highly competent cast, all of them, however, suffering from not enough to work with. What comes off best is Derek McLane’s brilliant design of a Greenwich Village basement pad in 1934. But this not being a musical, you can’t exit humming the scenery.

cn.t: Langella delivers a commanding, seductive performance as a villainous financier, but Rattigan's creaky 1963 melodrama proves too dated and hollow to fully support even this master actor's considerable talents.

sg.vl: Intimate 740-seat house, center orchestra is the premium pick
sg.ra: Headout and TickPick both name center orchestra rows C-H (seats 105-109) as the best unobstructed views in the 740-seat house; rows E-J are called out as the value sweet spot before mezz overhang begins at row H. TripAdvisor reviewer: 'had great seats (row 3) ... seats further back would have been good too' given the small theater size.

sg.vl: Under deep mezz overhang, top of stage cut off
sg.ra: Headout guidance: 'Avoid the last three orchestra rows (N, O, and P) and the extreme corner seats.' Corroborated by search finding that beyond row N 'seats experience cut-off at the top of the stage' due to the mezzanine overhang that starts at row H.

sg.vl: Overhead sightline into the set, better-than-average legroom
sg.ra: Headout: 'Mezzanine seats as close to the middle of rows A to C as possible offer fantastic overhead views of the stage which are perfect for impressive sets and sweeping action.' Headout also notes 'better than average legroom, which makes up for the lack of inside aisles.' BWW forum poster recommended Mezz Row A seats 109-110 as a strong option.
sg.rr: A-G (single curved section, ~257 seats, no center aisle)

sg.vl: Budget-friendly with clean sightlines in a small house
sg.ra: Headout: 'rear mezzanine offers budget-friendly options with a pretty good view of the stage for a lower price.' TripAdvisor reviewer sat 'in the very last row of the balcony at this beautiful old theater and had an excellent view' — small-house intimacy holds up to the back wall.
sg.rr: D-G (within the single A-G mezz; back rows cited)

sg.vl: Heavily obstructed per TripAdvisor and BWW forum
sg.ra: TripAdvisor reviewer on house-wide sightlines: 'Most seats have excellent views of the stage, apart from the box seats labeled as obstructed view ... When this theater says obstructed, it means obstructed -- not partially obstructed.' BWW forum user tombomb31 on the box seats: 'I'm pretty sure I remember hearing they're incredibly obstructed.' Search notes: 'Anything that is on the far side of the stage you are sitting on is obstructed.'
